title: Action principles, classical field theory and gauge fields
scope: General relativity and its matter as Lagrangian field theories: functionals and functional derivatives, Lagrangian densities and the stationary-action principle for fields, Euler-Lagrange field equations and boundary terms, the metric-variation toolkit (inverse metric, determinant, connection, Palatini identity), the Einstein-Hilbert action and its variation, Gibbons-Hawking-York and Palatini formulations, matter actions with the gravitational coupling and the Hilbert stress-energy tensor, Noether's theorem, canonical energy-momentum and diffeomorphism invariance as the origin of conservation, scalar (Klein-Gordon, complex, phi-fourth) and Maxwell field theories, spontaneous symmetry breaking with Landau theory and its field-theory consequences, and gauge theory with fibre bundles, connections and curvature as the language shared by electromagnetism and gravity. Particle Lagrangian mechanics, the stress-energy tensors that result, and Kaluza-Klein or quantum aspects belong to other domains.

concepts.title: Classical field theory
aliases: matter fields versus the metric field
concepts.summary: A classical field theory describes nature by fields, functions on spacetime giving a scalar, vector or tensor value at every event, obeying deterministic local equations without quantization. General relativity is such a theory: its fields are the matter fields and the metric itself.

names: matter fields versus the metric field

merged_from: matter fields versus the metric field
concepts.notes: GA stresses that GR has two classes of dynamical field: matter fields (scalar, electromagnetic, fluid) whose energy content forms T, and the metric, which carries geometry; a Lagrangian formulation must contain and couple both.

concepts.title: Functional
concepts.summary: A functional is a rule that takes an entire function as input and returns a single number; the action, which assigns a number to a whole history of a system, is the model example.

concepts.title: Functional derivative
concepts.summary: The functional derivative of an action with respect to a field is the quantity whose integral against a small change of the field gives the first-order change of the action; for a Lagrangian depending on a field and its first derivatives it equals the Euler-Lagrange expression, with an extra double-divergence term when second derivatives appear. The variation symbol obeys the rules of a derivative (linearity, Leibniz rule) and commutes with partial differentiation.
concepts.notes: DIV shows that for a metric theory the Euler-Lagrange derivative with respect to g_ab is a symmetric tensor density of weight +1, inferred from the invariance of the first-order change of the action. Commutation of variation and differentiation is what makes integration by parts possible.

concepts.title: Lagrangian density and field action
concepts.summary: A Lagrangian density is a local function of the fields and their first derivatives whose integral over space gives the Lagrangian and whose integral over spacetime gives the action of a field theory. In curved spacetime it must be a scalar density of weight one (a scalar times sqrt(-g)) so that the action is coordinate invariant.
concepts.notes: Worked example: a stretched string with Lagrangian density (rho/2)(d_t psi)^2 - (T/2)(d_x psi)^2, kinetic minus elastic energy per length (GA ch40). The particle action S = integral L dt of GA ch02 is owned by mechanics-and-newtonian-gravity (hamiltons-principle); here it is recorded only as the starting point that the field action generalizes. GA announces that "Lagrangian" means the density from ch40 on.

concepts.title: Principle of stationary action for fields
concepts.summary: The field configuration realized in nature is one for which the action does not change to first order under any small variation of the fields that vanishes on the boundary of the spacetime region considered. Applied to the metric as the varied field, the same principle yields Einstein's equations.

names: principle of stationary action for fields

merged_from: principle of stationary action for fields
concepts.notes: GA warns that the simple field version assumes the volume element is unaffected by the variation, which is exactly what fails when the metric is varied. The DIV ch08 statement for particle mechanics belongs to hamiltons-principle.

concepts.title: Boundary terms and total-divergence ambiguity
aliases: adding a divergence to the Lagrangian
concepts.summary: Integrating by parts in a variation produces a total divergence, which the divergence theorem turns into an integral over the boundary; it drops out when the variation vanishes there. For the same reason, two Lagrangian densities that differ by a total divergence give identical field equations.

names: boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert variation
total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
fixing the value does not fix the slope

merged_from: boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert variation
total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
concepts.notes: In the Einstein-Hilbert variation the term involving delta R_ab becomes the divergence of a vector density built from delta Gamma. The divergence ambiguity is what lets DIV replace sqrt(-g) R by the first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian. The particle-mechanics version of the ambiguity is recorded under lagrangian in mechanics-and-newtonian-gravity.

concepts.title: Euler-Lagrange equations for fields
concepts.summary: A field that makes the action stationary satisfies dL/dphi = d_mu[dL/d(d_mu phi)], one equation per field component; the time derivative of particle mechanics becomes a spacetime divergence. In curved spacetime the partial derivatives are replaced by covariant ones when the Lagrangian is written with a scalar Lagrangian and the invariant volume element.

names: field equations from a variational principle

merged_from: field equations from a variational principle
concepts.notes: GA derives the flat version by varying inside a region, integrating by parts and discarding the surface term, then obtains the curved-spacetime form by the comma-to-semicolon upgrade, also for each component of a vector field.

concepts.title: Hamiltonian density
concepts.summary: The Hamiltonian density of a field is the Legendre transform of its Lagrangian density, pi dphi/dt minus the Lagrangian density, where pi = dL/d(dphi/dt) is the momentum density conjugate to the field; it leads to first-order Hamilton equations for fields.
concepts.notes: Mechanics-and-newtonian-gravity owns the particle Hamiltonian from the same GA ch40 exercises and handed the density over to this domain.

concepts.title: Real scalar field theory
concepts.summary: The simplest field theory: one real number phi per event, with Lagrangian density -(1/2) g^{mu nu} d_mu phi d_nu phi - (1/2) m^2 phi^2 in signature (-+++) (sign conventions differ between books). Its quanta are spin-0 particles of mass m, and it is the standard test case for field equations, stress-energy and Noether currents.
concepts.notes: DIV uses signature (+---) and the neutral pion as its physical example. The stress-energy tensor of the scalar field is owned by matter-and-stress-energy (scalar-field-stress-energy-tensor).

concepts.title: Klein-Gordon equation
concepts.summary: The Klein-Gordon equation is the field equation of a free scalar of mass m, (box - m^2) phi = 0 with box = g^{mu nu} nabla_mu nabla_nu, obtained as the Euler-Lagrange equation of the scalar Lagrangian. Its static form with a source has the short-range Yukawa solution, which reduces to the long-range 1/r potential of Poisson's equation when m = 0.

names: Poisson's equation as the massless limit

merged_from: Poisson's equation as the massless limit
concepts.notes: The massless limit (static Klein-Gordon Green function becoming Poisson's) is the step GA ch47 uses to argue that long-range forces need massless carriers; the range-mass relation itself belongs to quantum-gravity-and-beyond. The legacy course adds the dispersion relation omega^2 = k^2 + mu^2 and flags mu = mc/hbar as extra quantum input.

concepts.title: Interaction Lagrangian
concepts.summary: When several fields are present, the total Lagrangian density is the sum of each field's free Lagrangian plus interaction terms containing products of different fields; these terms couple the fields, as J^mu A_mu couples a current to the electromagnetic potential and h_{mu nu} T^{mu nu} couples energy-momentum to a weak gravitational field.

concepts.title: Action of a charged particle
aliases: minimal coupling of a particle to a 1-form field
concepts.summary: The simplest Lorentz-invariant way for a field to influence a particle is to add q times the line integral of a one-form A_mu dx^mu along the world line to the free action -m integral dtau; the added term does not depend on how the path is parametrized, and varying the total action gives the Lorentz force law.

names: minimal coupling of a particle to a 1-form field

merged_from: minimal coupling of a particle to a 1-form field
concepts.notes: Distinct from the gravitational minimal-coupling rule (comma to semicolon) owned by equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Maxwell Lagrangian
concepts.summary: The electromagnetic field has Lagrangian density -(1/4) F_{mu nu} F^{mu nu} plus the coupling J^mu A_mu (in Heaviside-Lorentz-type units), with A as the varied field; its Euler-Lagrange equations are the sourced Maxwell equations, and varying it with respect to the metric gives the Maxwell stress-energy tensor.

names: Maxwell Lagrangian and electromagnetic stress tensor

merged_from: Maxwell Lagrangian and electromagnetic stress tensor
concepts.notes: DIV ch12 uses a first-order (Palatini-type) version in which the potential and F_ab are varied independently: one set of equations gives Maxwell's equations, the other defines F as the antisymmetrized derivative of the potential. GA ch48 recognizes the same term inside the reduced five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein action.

concepts.title: Variation with respect to the metric
concepts.summary: Varying an action with respect to the metric means computing its change under a small change delta g_{mu nu}; because the metric sits inside the volume element sqrt(-g), every raised index and the connection, each of these dependences must be varied explicitly rather than by quoting the matter-field Euler-Lagrange formula.

names: variation with respect to the metric

merged_from: variation with respect to the metric

concepts.title: Variation of the inverse metric
concepts.summary: Because g^{mu alpha} g_{alpha nu} is the fixed Kronecker delta, a change of the metric changes its inverse by delta g^{mu nu} = -g^{mu alpha} g^{nu beta} delta g_{alpha beta}: the indices are raised and a minus sign appears.
concepts.notes: The legacy course flags a common sign hazard: delta g^{mu nu} is not the variation delta g_{alpha beta} with its indices raised; they differ by a sign.

concepts.title: Variation of the metric determinant
concepts.summary: A change of the metric changes the volume density by delta sqrt(-g) = (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^{mu nu} delta g_{mu nu} = -(1/2) sqrt(-g) g_{mu nu} delta g^{mu nu}, a consequence of Jacobi's formula delta det M = det M tr(M^{-1} delta M).
concepts.notes: DIV's first test of the metric variational machinery is the Lagrangian sqrt(-g) alone: its Euler-Lagrange derivative is (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^ab, so on its own it would demand g^ab = 0; added to the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian it supplies the cosmological-constant term. The Jacobi formula itself is owned by mathematical-methods.

concepts.title: Variation of the connection
concepts.summary: Connection coefficients are not tensor components, but the difference between two connections is, so a first-order change delta Gamma^a_bc is a (1,2) tensor; for the metric connection it is given by the Christoffel formula with partial derivatives of g replaced by covariant derivatives of delta g.

names: variation of the connection in terms of the metric

merged_from: variation of the connection in terms of the metric
concepts.notes: Its tensor character is what allows the Palatini identity, first derived in geodesic coordinates, to hold in all coordinates.

concepts.title: Palatini identity
concepts.summary: For any change of the connection, the Riemann tensor changes by delta R^a_bcd = nabla_c(delta Gamma^a_bd) - nabla_d(delta Gamma^a_bc); contracting gives delta R_bd = nabla_a(delta Gamma^a_bd) - nabla_d(delta Gamma^a_ba), which makes g^bd delta R_bd a total divergence.
concepts.notes: DIV and the legacy course prove it at a point in geodesic coordinates, where curvature is a difference of connection derivatives, and extend it by tensor character; GA quotes it without proof.

concepts.title: Einstein-Hilbert action
concepts.summary: The Einstein-Hilbert action is the spacetime integral of the Ricci scalar weighted by the invariant volume element, S = (1/16 pi G) integral R sqrt(-g) d^4x (in c = 1 units); it is the simplest scalar action built from the metric that yields second-order field equations, and adding a constant to R gives the cosmological-constant term.
concepts.notes: GA justifies it only by covariance and simplicity. DIV writes it as gothic g^ab R_ab and notes that it contains second derivatives of the metric. Eddington's alternative sqrt(-g) R_abcd R^abcd appears only as a DIV exercise and illustrates that other curvature scalars give higher-order equations. Normalization conventions (c^3 versus c^4 prefactors) vary, as the legacy course warns.

concepts.title: Einstein equations from the action
aliases: variational derivation of the Einstein equations
concepts.summary: Varying the Einstein-Hilbert action with respect to the metric produces three pieces: the Ricci tensor from varying g^{mu nu}, minus half R g_{mu nu} from varying sqrt(-g), and a total divergence from the Palatini identity; discarding the boundary term, stationarity gives the vacuum Einstein equation G_{mu nu} = 0, and adding a matter action gives G_{mu nu} = 8 pi G T_{mu nu}.

names: vacuum Einstein equation from the action
variational derivation of the field equations
second-order nature of the Einstein equations
two variations make one field equation

merged_from: vacuum Einstein equation from the action
variational derivation of the field equations
second-order nature of the Einstein equations
concepts.notes: DIV does the variation three ways: brute-force expansion, the indirect route through the Palatini identity, and via the first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian; it also finds that the Euler-Lagrange derivative of sqrt(-g) R is -sqrt(-g) G^ab (sign by convention). The legacy course explains why an action linear in R gives second-order equations.

concepts.title: Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian
concepts.summary: Einstein's Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian is the part of sqrt(-g) R that is quadratic in Christoffel symbols; it differs from the Einstein-Hilbert density by a total divergence, so it depends only on the metric and its first derivatives and gives the same field equations, at the price of not being a scalar density.

concepts.title: Gibbons-Hawking-York boundary term
concepts.summary: Fixing the metric on a boundary does not fix its normal derivatives, so the Einstein-Hilbert action alone leaves a boundary contribution in its variation; adding twice the integral of the trace of the boundary's extrinsic curvature over the induced volume element cancels it and makes the variational problem well posed.

names: boundary term that refuses to disappear

concepts.notes: None of the three books treats it; it enters from the legacy course, whose toy model is S = integral q'' (fixed values but free slopes) and whose worked case is a cylinder r = R in Minkowski spacetime with K = 2/R. Corners and null boundaries need further terms.

concepts.title: Palatini formulation
concepts.summary: In the Palatini (metric-affine) approach the metric and a symmetric connection are varied independently in g^ab R_ab(Gamma) sqrt(-g); the metric variation gives the vacuum field equations, and the connection variation forces the connection to be metric compatible (in more than two dimensions), so the Levi-Civita connection is derived rather than assumed.

names: metric compatibility from the field equations

merged_from: metric compatibility from the field equations
concepts.notes: The legacy course lists exceptions where metric-affine and metric variations disagree: projective freedom, f(R) theories and matter coupled to torsion such as spinors.

concepts.title: Matter action and gravitational coupling
concepts.summary: The full action of general relativity is the Einstein-Hilbert action plus a matter action built from the non-gravitational fields and the metric; the relative weight (16 pi G in S = S_EH/16 pi G + S_M, with c = 1) is fixed by requiring the combined field equations to read G_{mu nu} = 8 pi G T_{mu nu}.

names: gravitational coupling constant in the action

merged_from: gravitational coupling constant in the action
concepts.notes: DIV writes the matter term with coupling 2 kappa and kappa = 8 pi G/c^4; GA introduces an undetermined constant alpha and finds alpha = 16 pi in G = c = 1 units. The value of the Einstein coupling constant from the Newtonian limit is owned by einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Hilbert stress-energy tensor
concepts.summary: The Hilbert (metric) stress-energy tensor is defined by how the matter action responds to a change of metric, T^{mu nu} = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta S_M/delta g_{mu nu}, equivalently T_{mu nu} = -2 dL_M/dg^{mu nu} + g_{mu nu} L_M for a scalar Lagrangian; it is symmetric and covariant by construction and is exactly the source that appears in Einstein's equations.

names: metric definition of the energy-momentum tensor

merged_from: metric definition of the energy-momentum tensor
concepts.notes: Sign conventions differ with signature: DIV (+---) writes delta L_M/delta g^ab = -(sqrt(-g)/2) T_ab. The factor of 2 is fixed by agreement with the canonical tensor for a scalar field in flat spacetime. Worked applications (scalar field, Maxwell field, complex scalar) produce tensors owned by matter-and-stress-energy. The legacy course warns that fluids and curvature couplings need extra care.

concepts.title: Canonical energy-momentum tensor
concepts.summary: The canonical energy-momentum tensor, [dL/d(d_alpha phi)] d^beta phi - g^{alpha beta} L, collects the four Noether currents of spacetime translations and is conserved in flat spacetime; unlike the Hilbert tensor it is generally not symmetric and not defined covariantly in curved spacetime, though for a scalar field the two agree.

concepts.title: Perfect fluid action
concepts.summary: A perfect fluid can be derived from the Lagrangian density equal to minus its total energy density, varied by displacing each flow line along a vector field while adjusting the rest-mass density to keep the particle current conserved; the resulting Hilbert tensor is the perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor.

names: flow-line variation by a displacement field

merged_from: flow-line variation by a displacement field
concepts.notes: GA holds the densitized current sqrt(-g) J fixed under metric variation, which fixes how the rest-mass density depends on the metric (the densitized current itself is owned by manifolds-and-metrics).

concepts.title: Symmetry of an action
concepts.summary: A symmetry of a field theory is a transformation of the fields, and possibly of the coordinates, under which the Lagrangian or action is unchanged (up to a boundary term), so the equations of motion are unchanged too; continuous families of such transformations are the input to Noether's theorem.

concepts.title: Noether's theorem
concepts.summary: Noether's theorem states that every continuous symmetry of an action yields a current with vanishing divergence on solutions, and hence a conserved quantity; for a scalar field and a symmetry generated by a Killing vector xi the current is [dL/d(d_alpha phi)] Lie_xi phi - xi^alpha L.
concepts.notes: GA derives it by dragging the Lagrangian along a vector field, treating the change as a Lie derivative and choosing a Killing field so the metric term drops. Spacetime translations give the canonical energy-momentum tensor; an x-translation is the worked example.

concepts.title: Diffeomorphism invariance
concepts.summary: General relativity is unchanged when every field, including the metric, is pushed along by a smooth map of spacetime to itself; configurations related this way are physically identical, so diffeomorphisms are the gauge symmetries of the theory, and an action built from a scalar density is exactly invariant under them.
concepts.notes: DIV uses it as a device: an infinitesimal relabelling of coordinates acts as a variation delta g_ab = Lie derivative of the metric, and the identically vanishing change of the action yields an identity (the contracted Bianchi identity for the gravitational Lagrangian).

concepts.title: Stress-energy conservation from diffeomorphism invariance
concepts.summary: If the matter action is unchanged when the metric is varied by a Lie derivative along any vector field, and the matter fields obey their own equations of motion, then the Hilbert stress-energy tensor has zero covariant divergence; local energy-momentum conservation is thus a consequence of diffeomorphism invariance rather than an extra postulate.

names: diffeomorphism invariance as origin of the conservation law
conservation of energy-momentum from diffeomorphism invariance

merged_from: conservation of energy-momentum from diffeomorphism invariance
diffeomorphism invariance as origin of the conservation law
concepts.notes: The same argument applied to the Einstein-Hilbert action gives the contracted Bianchi identity, which is how DIV ch11 uses it (ending with the fundamental lemma).

concepts.title: Global symmetry
concepts.summary: A global symmetry acts by the same amount at every spacetime point, for example multiplying a complex field everywhere by one constant phase e^{i alpha} or flipping phi to -phi everywhere; it contrasts with a local (gauge) transformation whose parameter varies from point to point.
concepts.notes: Worked example: the complex scalar Lagrangian is invariant under a constant phase because the conjugate field picks up the inverse factor.

concepts.title: Order parameter
concepts.summary: An order parameter is a macroscopic quantity that vanishes in the symmetric, high-temperature phase and becomes non-zero once a symmetry is broken, such as the magnetization of a ferromagnet or the equilibrium value of a scalar field.

concepts.title: Spontaneous symmetry breaking
concepts.summary: Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when the laws of a system (its Lagrangian or free energy) have a symmetry that its lowest-energy state lacks, so the system settles into one of several equivalent ground states (vacua) related by that symmetry; which one is picked is decided by small perturbations, not by the laws.
concepts.notes: GA builds the idea from a magnet and a buckling strut. The vacuum of a field theory is the uniform lowest-energy configuration at a minimum of the potential; several degenerate minima mean several vacua.

concepts.title: Landau theory of phase transitions
concepts.summary: Landau theory describes a continuous phase transition by expanding the free energy near the transition in even powers of an order parameter, F = F_0 + a M^2 + b M^4 with b > 0, where a changes sign at the critical temperature T_c; minimizing F gives M = 0 above T_c and a non-zero M below it.

concepts.title: Phi-fourth scalar field theory
concepts.summary: Phi-fourth theory is a real scalar field with potential U = (mu^2/2) phi^2 + (lambda/4!) phi^4 (lambda > 0), symmetric under phi -> -phi; for positive mu^2 the vacuum is phi = 0, while for negative mu^2 there are two degenerate vacua at nonzero phi, the field-theory version of Landau's transition.
concepts.notes: GA lets mu^2 depend on temperature, positive above T_c and negative below, so an expanding, cooling universe passes through symmetry breaking; this is asserted without finite-temperature field theory and prepares scalar fields for inflation (physical-cosmology).

concepts.title: Complex scalar field
aliases: phasor picture of a complex field
concepts.summary: A complex scalar field psi has Lagrangian density -(d_mu psi)*(d^mu psi) - m^2 |psi|^2 and can be written as an amplitude times a phase e^{i theta} at each point; it is the simplest theory with a U(1) phase symmetry and the standard model for charged matter in gauge theory.

names: amplitude-phase representation of a complex field

merged_from: amplitude-phase representation of a complex field

concepts.title: Mexican-hat potential
concepts.summary: The Mexican-hat potential for a complex scalar depends only on |psi|, with a local maximum at zero and a circle of degenerate minima at |psi| = |psi_0|; picking a ground state means picking a phase, which spontaneously breaks the U(1) symmetry.

concepts.title: Higgs mechanism
concepts.summary: In the Standard Model a scalar (Higgs) field acquires a non-zero vacuum value as the universe cools, breaking electroweak symmetry, separating electromagnetism from the weak force and giving mass to the W and Z bosons and to quarks and charged leptons.
concepts.notes: GA mentions it only as the real-world case that justifies studying scalar-field symmetry breaking in cosmology.

concepts.title: Topological defect
concepts.summary: A topological defect forms when a field settles into different vacua in different places and cannot join them smoothly; for a complex field whose phase winds by 2 pi around a point (a vortex, or a string in three dimensions), continuity forces the field magnitude to vanish at the core.

concepts.title: Internal variables and internal symmetry
concepts.summary: An internal variable is something a field carries at each point that is not a spacetime direction, such as the phase of a complex field or an isospin label; an internal symmetry transforms only these variables and moves nothing in spacetime.

concepts.title: Local gauge invariance
concepts.summary: Local gauge invariance demands that a theory be unchanged when its internal variables are transformed by a different amount at each point; because derivatives of the field then pick up extra terms, the demand can only be met by introducing a compensating gauge field.
concepts.notes: GA calls the bundle after a position-dependent transformation a "strained bundle", by analogy with atoms displaced by position-dependent amounts in a strained solid, and pairs it with a coordinate transformation in its gravity dictionary.

concepts.title: Gauge field
concepts.summary: A gauge field is a one-form A_mu introduced so that derivatives of a charged field transform covariantly under local internal transformations; under a local phase change it shifts by the gradient of the transformation parameter, and for U(1) with coupling q equal to the electric charge it is the electromagnetic potential.

concepts.title: Gauge covariant derivative
concepts.summary: The gauge covariant derivative D_mu = d_mu + i q A_mu removes the part of a charged field's change that is due only to the local phase convention, so that D_mu psi transforms exactly like psi; it is total change minus parallel-transport change, just as nabla is for tangent vectors.

concepts.title: Parallel transport of a charged field
concepts.summary: Moving a charged field value to a neighbouring point with no change except that dictated by the gauge connection rotates its phase by delta psi = -i q A_mu psi dx^mu; transport along a curve with D_mu psi = 0 is the bundle analogue of parallel transport (a horizontal lift).

names: parallel transport of a charged field

merged_from: parallel transport of a charged field

concepts.title: Gauge field strength
aliases: Faraday tensor as U(1) field strength
concepts.summary: The field strength of a gauge theory is the commutator of gauge covariant derivatives, [D_mu, D_nu]; it is gauge covariant and carries the physical content of the gauge field. For U(1) it equals i q F_{mu nu}, so the electromagnetic field tensor is the curvature of the phase bundle.

names: Faraday tensor as U(1) field strength

merged_from: Faraday tensor as U(1) field strength
concepts.notes: A GA exercise derives the gauge-field Bianchi identity (the cyclic sum of covariant derivatives of the field strength vanishes) from transport around a small cube or the Jacobi identity for covariant derivatives, mirroring the gravitational Bianchi identity.

concepts.title: Gauge theory
concepts.summary: A gauge theory is a field theory made invariant under local internal transformations by replacing ordinary derivatives with gauge covariant derivatives built from gauge fields; electromagnetism is the U(1) case, and the same structure underlies particle physics.

concepts.title: Yang-Mills theory
concepts.summary: A Yang-Mills (non-abelian) gauge theory has an internal symmetry group whose elements do not commute, so the gauge field is matrix-valued and its field strength contains a commutator of potentials besides their derivatives, making the gauge field self-interacting.

concepts.title: Fibre bundle
concepts.summary: A fibre bundle is a space built by attaching a copy of a fibre V above every point of a base manifold M, with a projection back to M, so that it looks locally like the product M x V; a field with internal variables is a choice of point in the fibre above each spacetime point, and for a complex phase the fibre is the U(1) circle.
concepts.notes: Because the phase of a single-valued complex field is defined only modulo 2 pi, the fibre is a unit circle (GA pictures a grid of knobs). GA ch48 recalls this picture for Kaluza-Klein theory, where the circle fibre becomes a real fifth dimension (owned by quantum-gravity-and-beyond).

concepts.title: Tangent bundle
concepts.summary: The tangent bundle TM of a manifold is the bundle whose fibre over each point is the tangent space there, so a point of TM is a point together with a tangent vector and dim TM = 2 dim M; a vector field is a choice of vector in each fibre.
concepts.notes: Example: the tangent bundle of the circle is the cylinder S^1 x R.

concepts.title: Trivial and twisted bundles
concepts.summary: Every bundle looks like a product over small regions of the base (local triviality), but it is trivial only if one product description M x V works globally; a twisted bundle such as the Moebius band is locally a product yet globally not, which can be detected by whether a section must meet the zero section.

concepts.title: Section of a bundle
concepts.summary: A section (cross section) of a bundle is a smooth choice of one point in the fibre above each base point, so fields are sections: a vector field is a section of the tangent bundle and the zero section picks the zero vector everywhere.
concepts.notes: Any section of the Moebius bundle must cross the zero section, whereas a section of the cylinder can avoid it.

concepts.title: Connection on a fibre bundle
concepts.summary: A connection on a bundle is the rule for comparing values in neighbouring fibres, deciding which change counts as no change when moving across the base; in U(1) gauge theory its components are i q A_mu, playing the role that Christoffel symbols play for tangent vectors.

concepts.title: Curvature of a bundle connection
concepts.summary: The curvature of a bundle connection is the two-form obtained from the commutator of its covariant derivatives; for the tangent bundle with the Levi-Civita connection it is the Riemann tensor, and for the U(1) phase bundle it is i q F.

concepts.title: Gravity-gauge theory analogy
concepts.summary: Gravity and electromagnetism share one geometric structure: coordinate transformations correspond to local phase changes, Christoffel symbols to the gauge potential, and Riemann curvature to the field strength F, all being connections and curvatures on bundles. The analogy has limits: the Einstein-Hilbert action is linear in curvature while Yang-Mills actions are quadratic.
concepts.notes: GA closes ch44 with a three-column table (GR / gauge theory / bundle). The legacy course compares the spin connection with F = dA + A wedge A and states where the analogy stops.
